title: Characterizing gene perturbations in single cells via network divergence analysis

paper_content.abstract: Functional perturbations of genes do not always cause expression changes, but can manifest through network rewiring or context-specific shifts in regulatory activity. However, inferring gene functional shift and linking them to the specific cell populations remains challenging, as most current scRNA-seq data analysis focuses either on differential gene expression or on cell abundance/state changes, but rarely associate gene perturbations with particular cell populations. Here we present scDNS, a framework that quantifies gene-specific functional perturbations by measuring information-theoretic divergence between condition-specific gene interaction network configurations. In simulated stress tests and multiple experimental datasets, scDNS prioritizes key regulators and the perturbed cell populations-even when mRNA changes are minimal but network rewiring is pronounced. Applications to immunodeficiency mutations, stimulus responses, and viral infection reveal hidden regulatory programs and heterogeneous responder cell states. In pancreatic cancer, scDNS nominates TIMM44 as a mitochondrial sensitizer enhancing gemcitabine efficacy. Together, scDNS provides a powerful tool for inferring dynamic gene perturbations on single cells.
paper_content.introduction:
Gene interaction networks (GINs) integrate multiple layers of molecular interactions, such as transcription factor-DNA binding, protein-protein interaction, and signaling pathways, to coordinate gene expression programs that define cellular identity, function, and adaptation to environmental stimuli. These networks exhibit inherent dynamism and modularity, wherein perturbations—including genetic mutations, infections, environmental stressors, or pharmacological agents—can alter regulatory relationships and modular structures, thereby reprogramming cellular states and phenotypes1,2. For example, the T95R mutation in IRF4 modifies its DNA-binding affinity, thereby restructuring its target gene network and resulting in defective B-cell maturation, reduced immunoglobulin class switching, and immunodeficiency3. Mutations in TP53 reorganize downstream transcriptional modules, yielding lineage-specific oncogenic outcomes that differ between epithelial and hematopoietic cells4. Pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), conventionally regarded as a glycolytic enzyme, undergoes striking remodeling of its interaction network upon activation of the EGFR–ERK pathway. Phosphorylation-dependent nuclear translocation enables PKM2 to relinquish its metabolic role and act as a transcriptional coactivator of β-catenin5. These cases highlight those perturbations extend beyond changes in gene expression, fundamentally restructuring the gene interaction networks that govern cellular processes. Thus, quantifying such network reorganizations will provide a valuable approach to deciphering how perturbations modify molecular circuits, identifying critical regulatory nodes, and elucidating adaptive mechanisms in disease progression and therapeutic responses.

Importantly, further mechanistic interpretation requires more than ranking “perturbed genes” alone: they also demand resolving in which cell states these regulators exert their effects—particularly when the perturbed program is confined to a specific cell subpopulation or manifests heterogeneously across cell states.

Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) have revealed the heterogeneous and dynamic nature of gene regulation across diverse cell types and states. This inherent complexity poses a significant challenge for comprehensively identifying functionally perturbed genes by simply reconstructing a universal GINs and analyzing network reconfiguration6,7. Current strategies for scRNA-seq analysis still predominantly rely on differential expression analysis (DEA) methods coupled with pathway enrichment analysis. Methods, such as Wilcoxon rank-sum or DESeq2-based methods, assess differences in mean expression or variance but fail to capture alterations in regulatory connectivity8,9. As a result, genes with unchanged expression yet profoundly modified regulatory associations often evade detection. Emerging DEA approaches, such as waddR10 and covariance-oriented frameworks like Memento11, capture distributional changes and gene-gene correlations. However, they remain insufficient for quantifying functional perturbations that specifically modulate gene-gene interactions. Similarly, regulon-centric tools like VIPER12 and SCENIC13 depend on predefined, static regulatory models. These methods often underperform in dynamic contexts where regulators and targets exhibit condition-specific rewiring, as exemplified by the IRF4 pT95R mutation3. Critically, even when a candidate regulator is nominated, existing pipelines rarely provide a principled way to map that regulator’s functional perturbation back onto individual cells, leaving the downstream cellular “footprint” of rewiring ambiguous. This disconnection limits mechanistic follow-up, because it becomes unclear whether a putative driver reflects a broad state transition, a rare responder subset, or a context-restricted program within a specific lineage.

Detecting cell populations subject to condition-specific perturbations represents an additional analytical challenge. Current strategies, including Milo14 (which evaluates differential abundance via k-nearest neighbor graphs), scDist15 (which quantifies donor-specific variability using mixed-effects models), MELD16 (which computes perturbation probabilities from density variations in latent space), and Augur17 (which employs machine learning to prioritize cell types based on separability across conditions), offer insights at the population level but primarily focus on compositional or broad transcriptional shifts rather than the underlying rewiring of interaction networks driving functional alterations. As a result, cell- and gene-focused analyses are often performed in parallel but remain decoupled: cell-state changes may be identified without linking to upstream regulators, and regulators may be prioritized without resolving their cell-state–specific effects. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a comprehensive computational framework that quantifies perturbation-driven GIN reorganization at both gene and cellular resolutions, incorporating prior biological knowledge while accounting for the heterogeneity characteristic of scRNA-seq data.

Here, we present scDNS, a computational platform that frames GIN remodeling as an information-theoretic divergence between network architectures across contrasting conditions. scDNS first assesses a gene's functional perturbation by quantifying dynamic alterations in its gene-gene dependency patterns, subsequently inferring the resultant effects on individual cells for detecting the perturbed cell populations. By coupling regulator-level rewiring with cell-resolved perturbation readouts, scDNS bridges upstream molecular drivers and downstream cellular consequences within a unified framework. In both simulated gene and cell perturbation tests, scDNS demonstrated superior sensitivity and robustness in detecting predefined perturbed genes and cells compared to current methods. Furthermore, application across diverse biological contexts—including DSP knockdown, concurrent mutations in TERT, TP53, and PDGFRA, IRF4pT95R-associated immunodeficiency, IFN-β stimulation in lupus-derived T cells, COVID-19 lung single-nucleus RNA-seq, and gemcitabine treatment in pancreatic cancer—consistently revealed previously overlooked perturbed regulators and delineated their cell-type-specific effects. We discovered the multifaceted effects of IRF4pT95R on B cells, natural killer (NK) and natural killer T (NKT) lineage development, upstream mediators of IFN-β-induced T-cell tolerance, alveolar cell susceptibilities in COVID-19 with therapeutic implications, and TIMM44 as a mitochondrial factor enhancing gemcitabine cytotoxicity. Collectively, these findings establish scDNS as a robust and versatile platform for quantifying functional perturbations within GINs. This capability significantly enhances our power to unravel the molecular basis of cellular responses, reveal previously latent regulatory processes, and ultimately accelerate the identification of therapeutic candidates across a wide array of biological systems.
paper_content.results:
Overview of scDNS
Gene interaction networks, comprising multifaceted molecular interactions such as protein-DNA binding, protein-protein interactions, and signaling cascades, underpin the orchestration of transcriptional programs in cellular systems. Perturbations, whether experimental or pathological, can profoundly remodel these networks by modulating gene-gene dependencies, inducing transcriptional reprogramming, and reorganizing modular connectivity. Quantifying such reconfiguration provides a rigorous approach to elucidating perturbation effects on cellular phenotypes and revealing core regulatory principles. We introduce scDNS, a computational framework that conceptualizes network reconfiguration as the information divergence between two conditions. It offers a robust metric to evaluate gene-level functional disruptions and to characterize the cellular consequences of perturbations under contrasting conditions. The methodology proceeds through three sequential stages.

The first step reconstructs a context-specific GIN by integrating prior biological knowledge with single-cell transcriptomic data to capture condition-dependent interactions (Fig. 1a). We employed a Graph Attention Network (GAT)18, a specialized Graph Neural Network (GNN), to refine an initial reference network assembled from curated regulatory interactions (TRRUST19 and Dorothea20), protein-protein interactions (IntAct21 and STRING22) and signaling pathway databases (KEGG23 and SuperPathway24) (see Methods). This integrated prior network covers >90% of genes detected in the human single-cell datasets analyzed in our study, and ablation analyses confirm that incorporating these curated databases improves scDNS’s ability to infer biologically meaningful perturbation signals (Supplementary Fig. 1a&b). The model represents the network as a graph G=(V, E), where vertices V correspond to genes and edges E denote regulatory interactions. Vertex features are encoded using node2vec25 to encode network topology, while edge features are represented by embeddings that integrate three attributes of neighborhood relationships. To train the GAT, we adopted a semi-supervised contrastive learning strategy by leveraging high-confidence positive and negative edge labels to guide model optimization. Positive edges were defined as those involving housekeeping genes (e.g., consistently expressed across cell types) or cell-type-specific markers (e.g., derived from scRNA-seq cluster annotations), enabling the model to learn both universal and cell type-specific interactions. Negative edges were assigned to pairs with zero geometric mean expression in scRNA-seq data or randomly sampled gene pairs lacking supporting evidence in prior knowledge databases. GAT is optimized using a composite loss function comprising: (1) an edge classification loss, which evaluates attention scores against labeled positives to prioritize biologically relevant interactions, and (2) a graph information loss based on Deep Graph Infomax (DGI)26, which maximizes the mutual information between the encoder representations of the original graph and a corrupted graph generated by randomly shuffling vertices and edges. To ensure robustness, the model is trained ten times, with attention scores aggregated to rank edge reliability. Edges consistently receiving high attention scores (top 80% by ranking aggregated score) were retained as strong, context-specific interactions, while the lowest 20% were pruned to eliminate noisy or spurious connections. This GAT-based network inference is stable, reproducible, and scalable, yielding robust attention patterns and reliable convergence across marker-gene choices, high-confidence edge construction, stochastic training runs, and upstream clustering/annotation variability (Supplementary Note 1). It effectively distinguished true interactions from random ones, achieving a high area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.99 (Supplementary Fig. 1c&d). This process yielded a refined GIN that balances universal regulatory interactions with cell-type-specific and condition-dependent edges, providing a robust foundation for downstream analyses.

The second step involves quantifying perturbation-induced alterations in gene–gene relationships within the refined GIN to identify regulatory genes across two contrasting conditions (Fig. 1b). To address data sparsity and heterogeneity inherent in single-cell data, we model the relationship between gene pairs using two complementary probability distributions: (1) a joint probability distribution that captures universal expression relationships prevalent in abundant cell populations, and (2) a conditional probability distribution that enhances sensitivity to regulatory shifts in sparse or transitional cell subpopulations27,28. Together, this dual-model framework encapsulates both global and context-specific gene-gene relationships (Supplementary Fig. 1e-h). The Jensen–Shannon Divergence (JSD) measures the information-theoretic distance of these distributions between the two conditions, enabling the detection of both broad and localized perturbations in gene expression patterns, and also providing insights into changes in cell population abundance or cell states. For each gene pair, the JSD value is weighted by the geometric mean of their expression levels to emphasize changes in transcriptionally active regions. The weighted JSD values are aggregated for each gene across its interacting partners to derive a functional perturbation score. To mitigate bias from heterogeneous regulatory module sizes, raw scores are transformed into degree-normalized Z-scores based on a null distribution derived from randomized networks.

The final step distributes each gene pair's JSD value to individual cells based on its pointwise divergence contribution (Fig. 1c). By summing the pointwise divergence contributions of all associated gene pairs for each gene, scDNS generates cell-specific perturbation scores that measure the impact of gene-level functional changes within each cell. All gene perturbation scores are then combined to compute a composite cellular effect score, which reflects the overall impact of perturbations on cell phenotypes, explaining changes in either cellular states or population proportions. In summary, scDNS quantifies functional perturbations at both gene and cellular levels by measuring network divergence across contrasting biological conditions, identifying key regulators and their responsive cell populations.

Systematic assessment of scDNS’s performance
We evaluated the performance of scDNS using both simulated and real scRNA-seq datasets. For stress testing, three simulated datasets were generated from iPSC-derived type 2 alveolar epithelial cells (iAT2) 29, H1 human embryonic stem cells (H1-hESCs), and PANC-1 cells30, respectively, with cells randomly assigned to control or in silico–perturbed groups. We perturbed each simulated dataset by modifying a subset of 100 genes under three biologically motivated regimes: (i) differential gene expression only (DGE), (ii) gene regulatory rewiring (DGR), and (iii) their combination (DGE+DGR); importantly, the simulation engine introduces these changes as structured, context-dependent perturbations to better mimic diverse, biologically realistic scenarios (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Note 2). To comprehensively characterize the problem difficulty and assess the power of our method to detect the perturbation signal, we generated ground truth case-control datasets by varying two key aspects. First, to further assess the effect of perturbation strength, we defined perturbed cells as hybrids of control cells and perturbed cells of variable relative weight (Methods). Decreasing the strength of the transcriptional difference between perturbed and unperturbed cells increased the difficulty of identifying the perturbed cell cluster. Second, perturbations were applied to varying fractions of cells, ranging from 10% to 100%. In these challenging scenarios, scDNS achieved accuracy exceeding 80% for either slight perturbation strength (>0.1) or a low fraction of perturbed cells (>10%) (Fig. 2b&c and Supplementary Fig. 2a). These results highlight the robustness of scDNS in detecting functionally perturbed genes, whether arising from altered expression levels or perturbations in gene-gene relationships.

We next assessed scDNS’s ability to recover perturbed cell subpopulations driven by diverse gene perturbations. In this validation setting, we artificially dysregulated 30 genes across three distinct subpopulations derived from the major cell clusters of the perturbed group. As an illustrative example, the perturbed subpopulations were not visually separated in the original UMAP embedding; however, incorporating the scDNS-derived perturbation scores (P-Score_cell) into the PCA embeddings successfully and clearly distinguished them (Fig. 2d & Supplementary Fig. 2b). The quantified stress tests across all three simulated datasets showed that scDNS maintains high accuracy even under weak and sparse perturbations (α = 0.25; 25% of cells perturbed), achieving AUC > 0.9 for perturbed-cell identification (Fig. 2e & Supplementary Fig. 2c).

To evaluate scDNS in real biological systems, we analyzed two scRNA-seq datasets: iAT2 cells with or without Desmoplakin (DSP) knockdown29, and H1-hESCs either wild-type or carrying triple mutations (TERTC228T + TP53G743A + PDGFRAD842V)31 (Fig. 2f). In both datasets, DSP (log₂FC = -0.27, false discovery rate (FDR) = 2.6 × 10⁻⁵, Wilcoxon test) and PDGFRA (log₂FC = 0.49, FDR < 6.4 × 10⁻384, Wilcoxon test) showed significant expression changes, therefore could be identified by standard differential expression analysis (e.g., Wilcoxon test), distributional differential expression methods (i.e., waddR), and Memento-de for evaluating differences in gene expression levels (Fig. 2g&h). However, the TP53 mutation did not significantly alter its expression (log₂FC = 0.05, FDR = 1, Wilcoxon test) but reconfigured its network of interacting genes (Supplementary Fig. 2d), rendering it undetectable by most conventional differential expression analyses. While Memento’s differential-variability module identified TP53, it failed to detect DSP and PDGFRA. Remarkably, scDNS was the only method capable of identifying all perturbed genes, including both differentially expressed and non-differentially expressed but network-perturbed genes. Furthermore, scDNS achieved superior accuracy compared with VIPER’s inferred protein activity analysis (99.8% vs. 70.5% for PDGFRA; 95.1% vs. 78.5% for DSP; 91.4% vs. 18.1% for TP53) (Supplementary Fig. 2e). Additional perturbed genes identified by scDNS were strongly enriched for biological processes associated with the phenotypes affected by these perturbed driver genes (Supplementary Fig. 2f). Despite its reliance on the reconstructed gene relationship network, scDNS exhibited remarkable robustness to the false-positive interactions, with a notable decline in accuracy only observed when the network contained more than 50% spurious interactions (Supplementary Fig. 2g). Moreover, scDNS demonstrated stable performance across genes with diverse degrees of network connectivity (Supplementary Fig. 2h&i).

We extended our validation by benchmarking scDNS against existing algorithms for detecting perturbed cells influenced by DSP knockdown or triple-gene mutations. For analyzing a single gene's perturbation effects, scDNS demonstrated superior discrimination between contrasting groups compared to metrics derived from inferred protein activity (VIPER) and raw gene expression levels (Fig. 2i). Furthermore, when assessing the overall perturbation effects across all genes, scDNS achieved the highest classification performance among all comparable methods (AUC = 0.99 for triple mutations dataset and 0.95 for DSP knockdown dataset) (Fig. 2j). Notably, Milo emerged as the second-best method, showing only slightly lower accuracy and specificity than scDNS (AUC = 0.92 for triple mutations dataset and 0.94 for DSP knockdown dataset). Collectively, these results robustly establish scDNS as a precise and powerful approach for identifying functionally perturbed genes and their affected cell populations across both simulated and real-world scRNA-seq datasets.

scDNS uncovers pleiotropic effects of IRF4 mutation on immune cells’ regulatory program and development
scDNS was applied to a single-cell RNA-seq profile of 18,640 B cells from healthy donors and individuals heterozygous for the IRF4pT95R mutation (Fig. 3a). The IRF4pT95R variant, which causes autosomal-dominant combined immunodeficiency (CID), preserves normal IRF4 mRNA and protein expression yet alters its canonical DNA-binding specificity, leading to a global rewiring of its regulatory network3. Such mutation-induced topological reconfigurations of gene–gene interactions exemplified the type of functional network perturbation that scDNS was designed to detect and quantify. Accordingly, scDNS pinpointed IRF4 as a significantly perturbed regulator (top 2%), characterized by significantly altered interaction relationships within its regulatory network (Supplementary Fig. 3a). This sensitivity contrasted with conventional single-cell analytical methods—such as Memento, waddR, and DEA—which either ranked IRF4 poorly or failed to detect its dysregulation, since the T95R mutation does not alter IRF4 mRNA abundance (log2 FC = -0.12, FDR = 1, Wilcoxon test) (Fig. 3b & Supplementary Fig. 3b). Even protein-activity inference methods like SCENIC only detected IRF4 dysregulation modestly (79% accuracy) (Supplementary Fig. 3c).

We observed that the perturbation score of IRF4 markedly elevated in plasmablast and plasma-cell subsets (Fig. 3c), consistent with the differentiation blockade reported in IRF4pT95R immunodeficiency3. However, Milo, MELD, and Augur were unable to identify this remarkable perturbation in plasma cell development except scDist (Supplementary Fig. 3d-f). To contextualize these perturbations, we reconstructed the B-cell differentiation trajectory (Fig. 3d) and mapped the scDNS-derived IRF4 perturbation scores across pseudotime (Fig. 3e). The scDNS method successfully captured functional perturbations even in early B cells, while metrics based on IRF4 gene expression and SCENIC activity were insensitive to these early changes, exhibiting weak changes (log2 FC < 0.1) (Fig. 3e). For quantitative validation, the IRF4 perturbation scores exhibited a strong correlation (R = 0.86, p = 2.2×10-16) with the aggregate expression of established IRF4-bound target genes identified by chip-seq data analysis, substantially exceeding the correlations obtained from gene expression (R = 0.49, p = 8.4×10-5) or SCENIC activity (R = 0.42, p = 9×10-4) (Supplementary Fig. 3g). Analysis of B cells before they commit to becoming plasmablasts and plasma cells revealed two distinct subpopulations (Fig. 3f), exhibiting differential expression of IRF4-bound target genes during B cell differentiation (Fig. 3g & Supplementary Fig. 3h). These two groups displayed an inverse relationship between IRF4 perturbation score and differentiation pseudotime, though they showed different perturbation levels (Fig. 3f). Specifically, one subpopulation underwent advanced differentiation despite minimal IRF4 perturbation (Fig. 3h). In contrast, the second group suffered from significantly stronger IRF4 dysfunction, leading to restricted differentiation. This suppression of differentiation was further supported by upregulation of key transcriptional repressors of B cell differentiation—including NOTCH232, BACH233, PAX534, and FOXO135 (Fig. 3i). This pattern ultimately indicates that B cells with mild perturbation proceed toward progressive differentiation, while those with strong perturbation remain arrested in immature states.

Beyond IRF4 itself, scDNS identified top 250 dysregulated genes, implicating pathways central to B-cell immunity and antiviral defense (Fig. 3j). Seventeen of these genes are annotated in Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database36 as causative for immunodeficiency syndromes. Significantly, all but one (SEC61A1) showed a positive correlation with the IRF4 perturbation score and were components of a relevant protein-protein interaction network (Fig. 3k). These results suggest that interacting proteins undergo co-modulatory or synergistic functional changes, implying shared underlying pathogenic mechanisms. This is exemplified by IRF8, a known IRF4 functional partner during early B-cell development37, which showed coordinated functional perturbations with IRF4 in the progenitor stages (Fig. 3l).

Extending beyond the B-cell compartment, analysis of the whole peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) dataset revealed that IRF4 dysfunction also perturbs the NK and NKT lineages, as evidenced by significantly elevated IRF4 perturbation scores (Fig. S3m&n). This finding contradicted the original clinical report, which found no alteration in NK-cell activation or abundance3. Our analysis further delineated the impact of IRF4 perturbation in the NK lineage, revealing a functional shift from short-lived effector cells (SLEC) toward memory-precursor cells (MPEC). This shift was transcriptionally characterized by the corresponding down-regulation of SLEC and up-regulation of MPEC gene signatures (Fig. 3o & Supplementary Fig. 3i). Collectively, these results demonstrate that scDNS is highly effective at pinpointing gene dysfunctions arising from pathogenic mutations and delineating their diverse impacts on cell differentiation across various immune lineages.

scDNS uncovers upstream regulators driving heterogeneous cellular responses to external stimuli in PBMCTs
To evaluate the value of scDNS in uncovering regulatory mechanisms of cell response to external stimuli, we applied it to a single-cell RNA-seq dataset of 13,999 PBMCs of 8 lupus patients treated or untreated with recombinant human IFN-β38 (Fig. 4a). IFN-β plays a central role in immune activation by interacting with the interferon alpha/beta receptor (IFNAR); however, its functional impacts across diverse cell types and developmental states remain incompletely understood. For perturbed genes identification, scDNS detected 2784 genes significantly responsive to IFN-β (adjusted p < 0.05) (Fig. 4b). Notably, IFNAR1—whose expression change was minimal (log2 FC = -0.13, Supplementary Fig. 4a)—was ranked much higher by scDNS (66th, 99.4%) than by conventional differential expression approaches. The best-performing DEA was memento’s differential-variability analysis (accuracy 88%), while differential analysis of VIPER-inferred protein activity reached 73% accuracy. These results underscore scDNS’s superior sensitivity for identifying direct treatment targets (Fig. 4c). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) further showed that scDNS-identified genes were strongly enriched in interferon-related pathways, including “cellular response to type I interferon” and “type I interferon signaling pathway” with stronger significance levels compared to alternative methods (Fig. 4d). This improvement arose because scDNS not only captured canonical transcriptional responses to IFN-β but also revealed upstream regulators of the signaling cascade that were missed by conventional gene expression analysis (Fig. 4e). For example, JAK1 and WTAP—despite showing negligible transcriptional changes under IFN-β stimulation (log₂FC = 0.01, Wilcoxon rank = 7551; log₂FC = 0.06, Wilcoxon rank = 8011) (Supplementary Fig. 4b) —were prioritized by scDNS (JAK1: scDNS rank=2263, FDR = 0.02; WTAP: scDNS rank=1692, FDR = 0.007). This observation suggested that IFN-β modulates their activity via non-transcriptional mechanisms. Indeed, IFN-β stimulates JAK1 activation through receptor-mediated autophosphorylation within the IFNAR–JAK–STAT signaling axis39. For WTAP, a recent study demonstrated that IFN-β induces its phase separation into liquid-like condensates, thereby modulating its role in m6A RNA methylation40. Consistently, we observed significant enrichment of scDNS-identified genes in related pathways governed by JAK1 and WTAP activity (Supplementary Fig. 4c).

We next examined cell type–specific effects of IFN-β treatment across 8 annotated clusters. By mapping scDNS-derived integrated sc-Zscores onto the UMAP embedding, we observed heterogeneous responses, indicating distinct sensitivities of individual cell states to IFN-β stimulation (Fig. 4f). CD4+ T cells and monocytes exhibited relatively stronger responses than other cell types, with high variability (Fig. 4g). In monocytes, scDNS revealed a significant and stronger response to IFN-β in CD14+ (classical) subpopulations than CD16+ (non-classical intermediate) monocytes, aligning with prior studies41, whereas MELED and Milo did not detect this difference (Supplementary Fig. 4d-h). Within CD4+ T cells, memory and naïve subsets were the most responsive, while activated states showed less perturbation (Fig. 4h). Beyond shared responsive genes, scDNS identified distinct mechanisms across three subsets, with memory cells upregulating genes associated with antigen processing and presentation, while naïve cells responded primarily through T cell proliferation (Fig. 4i). Importantly, scDNS revealed that activated T cells responded through the induction of cell tolerance, a key mechanism in lupus treatment. The majority of these responsive genes were not detected by standard differential expression analysis. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that scDNS is a valuable tool for discovering key upstream regulators of cascade signaling pathways and heterogeneous cellular perturbations in response to external treatments.

scDNS identifies cellular vulnerabilities and therapeutic targets in COVID-19
To further assess scDNS’s accuracy in the presence of cohort effects (i.e., individual-to-individual variation), we applied it to lung single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) data from 19 COVID-19 patients who succumbed to severe infection and 7 healthy donors42(Fig. 5a). scDNS assigned higher ranks to 1738 host genes known to interact with SARS-CoV-2 RNA and viral proteins, with their perturbation scores exceeding those of other genes (Fig. 5b). Based on the aggregated perturbation score of these host genes, we found that SARS-CoV-2 exerted a significantly high perturbation effect on alveolar type 1 (AT1) and alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells (Fig. 5c & Supplementary Fig. 5a). This finding aligns with the well-established role of alveolar epithelial cells as the primary host cells for SARS-CoV-243. Notably, scDNS-prioritized genes showed significant enrichment in phosphoproteomic and proteomic signatures detected from SARS-CoV-2–treated Vero E6 cell lines in vitro44, with enrichment scores rising with treatment duration (Supplementary Fig. 5b). These findings demonstrate scDNS’s ability to identify genes with functional roles at the translational and post-translational levels.

At a finer resolution, scDNS revealed heterogeneous effects of SARS-CoV-2 on AT2 cells, characterized by a functional gradient ranging from low to high perturbation scores (Fig. 5d). Cells with high perturbation scores exhibited significant upregulation of 616 genes that can be considered as a transcriptional signature of severely infected cells (Fig. 5e). These signatures were enriched in pathways critical for SARS-CoV-2 survival and replication, including antigen presentation, protein translation, viral replication, and life cycle regulation (Supplementary Fig. 5c). Among these, we identified elevated expression of secretory leukoprotease inhibitor (SLPI) in cells with high perturbation scores (Fig. 5e). Spatial transcriptomics45 revealed that AT2 cells with these signatures were primarily located in bronchial-proximal regions (Fig. 5f), highlighting this niche as a key site of SARS-CoV-2 infection. This spatial-functional relationship was underscored by increased SLPI expression, an anti-protease predominantly produced in the airway46 (Fig. 5g). We further applied scDNS to immune cells, revealing pronounced heterogeneity in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection (Supplementary Fig. 5d). Signature genes from cells with high perturbation scores were mapped onto bulk PBMCs RNA-seq data from 274 COVID-19 patients47, showing that signatures of CD4⁺ T cells, CD8⁺ T cells, cycling NK/T cells, and dendritic cells increased markedly with disease severity—more prominently than genes identified by direct case–control comparisons (Supplementary Fig. 5d-h). Functional enrichment analysis further demonstrated that these upregulated signatures were significantly enriched in inflammatory pathways, COVID-19 infection–related signaling cascades, and previously reported severity-associated gene program (Supplementary Fig. 5i-k, Supplementary Data 1 and Supplementary Note 3). These signatures increased markedly with disease severity, establishing a strong link between transcriptional dysfunction of these signatures and COVID-19 progression.

To assess the therapeutic potential of scDNS-prioritized genes, we evaluated the antiviral activity of drugs and compounds targeting them. For this analysis, we utilized antiviral efficacy profiles of ~10,000 approved drugs and compounds from the NCATS COVID-19 portal and linked each compound to its targets using DrugBank annotations. Across NCATS assays, only 40% of drugs showed antiviral activity, and this proportion increased modestly to 45% when we restricted to virus-interacting host proteins (Fig. 5h). In contrast, prioritizing targets by scDNS based on high perturbation scores with increasingly stringent thresholds substantially improved success rates, reaching 56% among the top 50 genes and 62% when further limited to those host genes directly interacting with SARS-CoV-2. Furthermore, projection of scDNS-nominated genes onto drug–target interaction networks identified 76 genes linked to 257 candidate compounds, all of which exhibited anti–SARS-CoV-2 activity in at least two NCATS assays (Fig. 5i). These compounds included modulators of viral replication and host immune signaling pathways, providing a diverse repertoire of translationally promising therapeutic options. Collectively, these findings highlight scDNS as an effective framework for prioritizing therapeutic candidates in cohort dataset analysis, while reducing the risk of failure.

scDNS identifies TIMM44 as a regulator sensitizing pancreatic cancer cells to gemcitabine
To demonstrate the ability of scDNS to facilitate novel biological discovery, we applied it to a scRNA-seq dataset of 1,749 in vitro PANC-1 pancreatic cancer cells subjected to gemcitabine treatment or vehicle control30 (Fig. 6a). scDNS identified 2669 genes implicated in gemcitabine’s mechanism of action (MoA). The top-enriched pathway was the DNA damage response, consistent with gemcitabine’s well-established function in inhibiting DNA replication and inducing DNA damage through incorporation into DNA and depletion of deoxyribonucleotide pools (Fig. 6b). Notably, scDNS successfully prioritized the known gemcitabine targets RRM1 and RRM2 as the 44th and 27th most perturbed genes, respectively. In addition, 448 highly ranked genes were linked to cell-cycle regulation and DNA repair, 23 of which have been experimentally confirmed to contribute to gemcitabine’s MoA (Fig. 6c). For example, CHK1, a central mediator of gemcitabine-induced DNA damage signaling48, showed minimal differential expression (log2 FC = 0.14, FDR = 1, Wilcoxon test) yet a strong perturbation score (Z-score = 6.3, FDR = 2.1×10-8), highlighting scDNS’s ability to capture functional disruptions beyond expression changes. Beyond canonical DNA damage pathways, scDNS also revealed non-canonical effects of gemcitabine on mitochondrial function (Fig. 6d). Among these, SIRT1 (DEA: log2 FC = 0.18, FDR = 0.06, Wilcoxon test; scDNS: Z-score = 6.3, FDR = 2.5×10-14), an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase that promotes mitochondrial biogenesis and redox homeostasis, was markedly perturbed and has been reported to mediate gemcitabine’s MoA49.

Based on cell-level perturbation scores, we identified six cellular subpopulations exhibiting distinct responses to gemcitabine, with cluster 3 showing the strongest perturbation (Fig. 6e). Projection of each subpopulation’s transcriptional signature onto TCGA pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD) patient survival data revealed significantly different survival outcomes, where the signatures of cluster 3 are associated with the poorest prognosis (hazard ratio = 1.76, p = 3.3 × 10⁻5, two-sided Wald test) (Fig. 6f). In contrast, clusters defined solely by gene expression showed weaker prognostic stratification (Supplementary Fig. 6a&b). Cluster 3 was characterized by metastatic potential, impaired apoptotic regulation, and enhanced invasiveness (Fig. 6g). Genes with the highest perturbation scores in cluster 3 were enriched for cell-cycle and mitochondrial functions (Fig. 6h). Among them, SDHA (succinate dehydrogenase complex flavoprotein subunit A) was the most differentially perturbed gene (Fig. 6i). SDHA deficiency leads to succinate accumulation, which has been implicated in drug resistance through ubiquitin-cullin pathway dysregulation in several cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia50. The second-most perturbed gene, TIMM44, a core component of the presequence translocase-associated motor (PAM) complex of the mitochondrial inner membrane, exhibited no significant change in expression (log2 FC = 0.33, FDR = 1, Wilcoxon test) but a marked perturbation in network activity (Z-score = 9.0, FDR = 1.1×10-15) (Fig. 6i). Western blot analyses confirmed stable TIMM44 expression before and after gemcitabine treatment (Supplementary Fig. 6c). Complementary proteomics/phosphoproteomics further showed stable total TIMM44 protein but a significant increase in S180 phosphorylation after treatment (FC = 2.6, p = 0.006, two-sided t-test) (Supplementary Fig. 6d). S180 maps to a functionally important domain involved in TIMM44’s association with the translocon and recruitment of the mtHsp7051, and is supported as a bona fide regulatory site by recurrent detection in PhosphoSitePlus and strong evolutionary conservation (Supplementary Fig. 6e–g). These orthogonal data are consistent with a potential activity or interaction-state shift of TIMM44, providing supportive evidence for its prioritization by scDNS even in the absence of differential expression. Independent bulk RNA-seq datasets from TCGA and GTEx showed abnormally elevated TIMM44 expression in tumor versus normal tissues, indicating its potential as a therapeutic target (Supplementary Fig. 6h). Similarly, an independent single-cell dataset52 confirmed TIMM44 upregulation specifically in tumor cells (Supplementary Fig. 6i), supporting its potential as a tumor-selective target with low off-target-risk.

To experimentally validate TIMM44-mediated sensitization to gemcitabine, we performed in vitro combination assays using gemcitabine and the mitochondrial import inhibitor MitoBloCK-10 (MB-10). MB-10 potentiated the cytotoxic effect of gemcitabine (Fig. 6j & Supplementary Fig. 6j). At low gemcitabine concentrations (≤8 μM), the combination of MB-10 and gemcitabine exhibited a synergistic effect with an average Chou–Talalay combination index (CI) of 0.44. Transcriptomic profiling revealed that gemcitabine induced major transcriptional changes, further amplified in the gemcitabine + MB-10 combination (Fig. 6k). Differential expression analysis showed that downregulated genes were enriched for cell-cycle and DNA repair pathways. Notably, several of these genes—including SIRT149, DUSP153, EP30054, and MCL155—have been previously implicated in gemcitabine resistance Fig. 6l&m). Collectively, these results demonstrate that scDNS effectively delineates heterogeneous drug responses, identifies non-canonical perturbation mechanisms, and uncovers novel sensitivity-associated genes such as TIMM44, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target for improving gemcitabine efficacy.
paper_content.methods:
Context-adaptive GINs reconstruction
A semi-supervised analysis framework based on graph attention networks was designed to identify context-adaptive regulatory networks by integrating single-cell transcriptomic data with a comprehensive prior knowledge network. The overall analysis pipeline was comprised of the two steps:
(1) Prior knowledge network construction: A comprehensive biological networks encompassing gene regulatory interactions (GRIs), protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and signaling pathways was firstly constructed. The GRIs were sourced from the TRRUST database19 and the R Dorothea package (v1.7.4)20. PPIs were obtained from the IntAct21, and STRING databases22. Signaling pathways were collected from the KEGG23 and SuperPathway24 databases. In total, 332,740 unique interactions involving 21,006 genes were collected.
(2) Pre-set the high-confidence positive and negative edges: Standard Seurat preprocessing was applied to the single-cell RNA sequencing data to identify major cell types. Positive edges were defined as those connecting highly expressed and biologically relevant gene pairs within each cell type. Specifically, the COSG57 method was used to identify the top 100 marker genes for each cell type. In addition, housekeeping genes with an expression frequency greater than 75% and average expression above 1 were incorporated. These genes, along with their interactions in the prior knowledge network, were classified as positive interactions for each cell type. Negative edges were defined as (i) gene pairs exhibiting a geometric mean expression of zero across all cell types, and (ii) those randomly sampled pairs lacking prior biological evidence of interaction.

Node and edge encoding
Node embeddings for the prior knowledge network were obtained by applying the Node2Vec algorithm to map each vertex 𝑖 to a 512-dimensional vector 𝐡⃗⃗⃗_𝑖. This process captured both local neighborhood structure and global topological properties. For a candidate edge between genes 𝐺_𝑖 and 𝐺_𝑗 in cell population 𝐶_𝑘, the edge feature vector was constructed by integrating: (i) cell-specific co-expression 𝑓_exp(𝐺_𝑖,𝐺_𝑗,𝐶_𝑘), defined as the geometric mean expression of gene pair within 𝐶_𝑘; (ii) global co-expression statistics 𝑓_MI(𝐺_1,𝐺_2) and 𝑓_DREMI(𝐺_1,𝐺_2), computed as mutual information (MI) and density-resampled mutual information (DREMI) between genes across the whole dataset, log-transformed and sigmoid-normalized; and (iii) contextual features (𝑓_context(𝐺_1,𝐺_2)), a one-hot encoding of biological context (e.g., cell identity and treatment). The final edge feature vector is therefore 𝐡⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗_𝐺_𝑖,𝐺_𝑗,𝐶_𝑘 =[𝑓_exp,𝑓_DREMI,𝑓_MI,𝑓_context] (1).

Graph attention mechanism for context-adaptive regulatory network prediction
A GATv2-based graph attention encoder was employed to couple with a joint contrastive learning module. This module incorporates graph-level representation learning using Deep Graph Infomax (DGI) and an attention score-based edge supervision mechanism.

GAT encoder module: For a cell-type-specific gene network 𝐺=(𝑉,𝐸), where 𝑉 is the node set and 𝐸 is the edge set representing potential interactions 𝑒_𝑖,𝑗,𝐶_𝑘 between genes 𝑔_𝑖 and 𝑔_𝑗 in cell type 𝐶_𝑘, these edges were used employed for joint encoding. Given the node input feature 𝐡⃗⃗⃗_𝑖 and edge feature 𝐡⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗_𝐺_𝑖,𝐺_𝑗,𝐶_𝑘, the features are linearly transformed using the learnable weight matrices 𝑊_𝑣 ∈ℝ^{|𝑉|×𝐹′} and 𝑊_𝑒 ∈ℝ^{|𝐸_all|×𝐹′}, where 𝐹′ is the embedding dimension, and |𝐸_all| is the total number of edges across all cell type networks. Then, the attention score for the message propagation from node 𝑗 to node 𝑖 in cell type 𝐶_𝑘 was calculated as:
𝛼_𝑖,𝑗,𝐶_𝑘 =Tanh(𝑎⃑^𝑇[𝑊_𝑣𝐡⃗⃗⃗_𝑖+𝑊_𝑣𝐡⃗⃗⃗_𝑗+𝑊_𝑒𝐡⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗_𝑖,𝑗,𝐶_𝑘]) (2)
where 𝑎⃑ is a learnable attention vector, and Tanh is the hyperbolic tangent activation function. This score reflects the importance of the neighbor 𝑗 and its connecting edge to the representation of node 𝑖. A Softmax normalization is applied over all incoming edges to node 𝑖 to obtain the normalized attention weight
𝛼′_𝑖,𝑗,𝐶_𝑘 =Softmax_𝑗∈𝑁_𝑖 (𝛼_𝑖,𝑗,𝐶_𝑘) (3).
This normalized score is used for weighted aggregation during message passing and serves as a proxy for the edge existence probability in the next supervised task.

Joint contrastive learning module: The model's GAT encoder was jointly optimized using both unsupervised contrastive learning and supervised edge classification. Deep Graph Infomax (DGI) is utilizedto learn structure-aware node embeddings 𝑍=𝑓_GATv2(𝑉,𝐸). This is achieved by maximizing the mutual information between the node representations 𝑍 and the graph-level summary vector 𝑠=sigmoild(mean(𝑍)), while minimizing the mutual information between the corrupted graph's node representations 𝑍̃ (generated by randomly shuffling input node features) and the summary 𝑠. The DGI loss is defined as:
ℒ_DGI =−𝐸_𝑍,𝑍̃ [log𝜎(𝑧^𝑇𝑠) + log(1 − 𝜎(𝑧̃^𝑇𝑠))] (4).
This loss ensures the model can distinguish the true graph structure from structural noise
Additionally, the normalized attention weights serve as the prediction 𝑦̂_𝑖,𝑗,𝐶_𝑘=𝛼′_𝑖,𝑗,𝐶_𝑘 for the ground-truth labeled edges 𝑦 (1 for positive interactions and 0 for negative ones). Focal Loss is employed to mitigate the severe positive/negative sample imbalance:
ℒ_edge classification = −𝛼(1-ŷ)^𝛾log(𝑦̂) − (1−𝛼)(1-y)𝑦̂^𝛾log(1−𝑦̂) (5)
Hyperparameters α and γ were set to 0.75 and 1.5, respectively, ensuring that the model focused on hard-to-classify samples. The final overall training objective is the weighted sum of the supervised and self-supervised losses:
ℒ_total =ℒ_edge classification + 𝜆∙ℒ_DGI (6)
The weight coefficient 𝜆 was set to 0.1 to balance the two objectives.

Training and edge prediction: Prior networks for each cell type across different conditions were integrated into a multiplex graph as the GAT input, allowing each gene pair to have multiple edges representing diverse cellular contexts. This design enables the model to simultaneously learn interaction patterns across these contexts. To enhance the model robustness and reproducibility, we independently trained the model across 10 random seeds. For each cell type, the attention scores for each edge across the 10 training runs were aggregated, and their Rank Product (RP) was then computed. The final ranking of gene interactions for each cell type was derived by independently sorting the edges based on their RP. To ensure high-confidence gene interactions, the minimum rank across all cell types was employed as a final evaluation criterion. Gene interactions that consistently ranked in the lowest 20% across all cell types were considered to have a low likelihood of occurring in the single-cell data system.

Estimate the perturbation scores for genes and cells
scDNS characterized the dynamic relationships of gene pairs in the network (G_i↔G_j) using joint and conditional gene expression probability densities. Each method had distinct advantages in capturing interactions within both high-density and low-density cell populations, allowing for a comprehensive analysis. The distribution densities were estimated based on a k-nearest neighbor (KNN) approach on a two-dimensional grid, following the widely used procedure of van Dijk et al28. A small random expression value was incorporated to improve robustness against extreme distributions, such as the zero-inflated distribution frequently observed in single-cell data.

Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) was utilized to quantify changes in probability densities across conditions. It provided valuable insights into both local and global information divergences between two probability distributions, providing a robust metric for assessing gene interaction dysregulation. To emphasize biologically relevant interactions, point-wise JSD was weighted by gene expression levels. The statistical significance of JSD was determined using a null distribution generated from 2×10^4 JSD values derived from randomized gene pairs not included in known interaction networks, with additional randomization of gene expression within each condition to account for background variability.

Finally, gene prioritization was performed at both global and single-cell levels. The significance of JSDs associated with a given gene was aggregated while accounting for network degree to avoid bias. Z-scores from joint and conditional probability densities were then combined to obtain an overall gene-level Z-score. Finally, single-cell Z-scores (sc-Zscores) were computed to quantify each gene’s effector cells based on weighted point-wise JSD. A detailed description of the algorithm was provided in the Supplemental information.

Simulation setup for benchmarking datasets
Three simulated datasets were generated from iAT2, H1-hESCs, and PANC-1 cells, with cells randomly assigned to control or in silico–perturbed groups. Perturbations were applied to a subset of 100 target genes under three biologically motivated regimes: (i) expression-only changes (DGE), (ii) rewiring-only changes affecting regulatory relationships or expression patterns (DGR), and (iii) coupled expression and rewiring changes (DGE+DGR). For rewiring changes, the relationships between each target gene and its partner genes were systematically modified to simulate context-dependent regulatory changes, including activation/inactivation and switches between positive and negative regulation. Only the top 60% of partner genes, ranked by their average Spearman correlation with other partners, were selected for rewiring. Perturbations were constrained within local neighborhoods and functional modules to preserve structured and biologically plausible alterations, enabling benchmarking of scDNS under realistic regulatory complexity. Expression-level perturbations were simulated by multiplying the expression of each target gene in perturbed cells by a factor of two. Combined perturbations were generated by applying both expression-level and rewiring changes simultaneously.

To systematically assess the effect of perturbation strength, perturbed cells were defined as hybrids between control cells and fully perturbed cells. We introduced a perturbation strength parameter, α (ranging from 0 to 1), to control the similarity between perturbed and control expression profiles. The resulting expression profile of each perturbed cell was computed as:
𝐸_𝛼 =(1−𝛼)·𝐸_before perturbation +𝛼·𝐸_after perturbation (7)
where 𝐸_before perturbation and 𝐸_after perturbation represent the expression profiles of the control and perturbed cells, respectively. Perturbation strength α was varied to create a gradient of transcriptional differences, simulating conditions ranging from subtle to strong perturbations. We additionally varied the fraction of cells subjected to perturbation from 10% to 100% to assess scDNS’s sensitivity across different levels of heterogeneity.

To further evaluate scDNS’s ability to detect subpopulation-specific perturbations, we first performed clustering of the single-cell data to define independent cell subpopulations. For three selected subpopulations, we then applied DGR, DGE, and combined perturbations to 30 high-expression marker genes per subpopulation, simulating biologically relevant perturbation scenarios across distinct cell clusters.

Comparison of perturbation detection methods
Gene-level perturbation analysis was performed using waddR (v1.15.0)10, memento (v0.1.1)11 in two modes (memento_de and memento_dv), and Seurat’s FindMarkers function (v4.3.0)58, including the following statistical frameworks: Wilcoxon rank-sum test, bimod likelihood-ratio test, ROC-based marker identification, Student’s t-test, negative binomial and Poisson generalized linear models, logistic regression, and MAST hurdle model. Cell-level perturbation detection was conducted using MELD (v1.0.2)16, Milo (v2.5.1)14, Augur (v1.0.3)17, and scDist (v1.1.4)15.

scRNA-seq data pre-processing
The Seurat R package (v4.3.0)58 was utilized to preprocess the scRNA-seq data. Following standard quality control procedures in single-cell data analysis, low-expression genes were filtered out and then normalized using the NormalizeData function with default parameters. Highly variable genes were identified using the FindVariableFeatures function with the default “vst” method. Subsequently, the principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to the scaled gene expression of highly variable genes. The datasets exhibiting batch-related differences were integrated using the Harmony R package (v0.1.0)59 with default parameters. The first 30 PCs were used to construct a shared nearest neighbor graph for cells and to identify cell clusters using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions, respectively. The clustering results were visualized using UMAP by the RunUMAP function. Cell annotation was performed using marker genes derived either from the original dataset or from a curated reference. Marker genes for each cluster were identified with the FindAllMarkers function with the “wilcox” method.

Single-cell protein activity inference
Single-cell transcriptomic data were first clustered to define coherent cell subpopulations. For each cluster, pseudo-bulk gene expression profiles were generated by averaging the expression of constituent single cells. Gene regulatory networks were reconstructed from these pseudo-bulk profiles using ARACNe60 for identifying the downstream targets (regulons) of each protein. Single-cell protein activity was subsequently inferred using the VIPER R package61. Proteins with small regulon size (<20 target genes) were excluded. Differences in protein activity between groups were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

Analysis of the expression levels of IRF4 target genes
The IRF4T95R-specific regulatory network was constructed using differential ChIP-seq peaks and expressed genes between IRF4T95R and wild-type samples (data available in reference3). The target genes of IRF4T95R were defined as those exhibiting an absolute log fold change greater than 1 in both gene expression levels and normalized peak counts. We classified the target genes into positive and negative regulators based on their upregulation and downregulation in expression levels. The regulatory network of IRF4pT95R was then employed to infer its specific abnormal activity in each cell through enriched regulon analysis implemented by the viper function in the viper R package (v1.28.0)61. IRF4 transcriptional activity was inferred using the pySCENIC Python package (v0.12.1)13. Pseudotime and stemness analyses of IRF4 p.T95R B cells were performed using Monocle3 (v1.3.1)62 and CytoTRACE (v 0.3.3)63 with default parameters.

Survival analysis
Cluster-specific marker genes (|log FC| > 0.25, adjusted p < 0.01) were identified from gemcitabine-treated single-cell data using the FindAllMarkers function in R Seurat. To evaluate clinical relevance, we retrieved TCGA pancreatic adenocarcinoma (TCGA-PAAD) raw count matrices and associated clinical metadata through the R TCGAbiolinks package (v2.35.3)64. Each cluster’s highly expressed genes were treated as a transcriptional signature and projected onto bulk tumor profiles by computing sample-level signature enrichment/activity scores using the VIPER algorithm (R viper package (v1.32.0)61), producing one quantitative score per signature per sample. Associations between signature scores and patient outcome were assessed using univariate Cox proportional-hazards regression with the R survival package (v3.5-3)65; signature score was modelled as a continuous covariate and results are reported as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals.

Cell culture and drug treatment
Human pancreatic adenocarcinoma cell line, PANC-1 cells (CL-0184, Wuhan Pricella Biotechnology Co., Ltd.), was cultured in DMETM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2. Cells were seeded in 96-well plates (3 × 10³ cells/well) and allowed to adhere overnight. Then, cells were treated with MitoBlock-10 (HY-115467, MedChemExpress) and gemcitabine (HY-17026, MedChemExpress), separately or in combination, for 72 h. Cell viability was assessed using the CCK-8 assay (C0037, Beyotime Biotechnology. Briefly, 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent was added to each well and incubated for 2 h at 37°C. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Background absorbance from blank wells was subtracted. Experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates.

Drug interactions were evaluated by calculating the combination index (CI) using the Chou-Talalay method (https://www.combosyn.com/). CI values were calculated using Compusyn software based on dose–response curves generated from multiple drug concentrations. CI < 1 indicates synergy, CI = 1 indicates an additive effect, and CI > 1 indicates antagonism.

For Western blot analysis, cells were treated with gemcitabine at indicated concentrations. Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined using a BCA protein assay. Equal amounts of protein (20 μg per lane) were separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk for 1 h at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4°C with anti-TIMM44 antibody (A21141, Abclonal; 1:1,000 dilution). After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (1:5,000 dilution) for 1 h at room temperature. Signals were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL). TIMM44 protein abundance was detected using anti-TIMM44 antibody (A21141, Abclonal) and HRP-conjugated secondary antibody, with visualization by ECL. Protein levels were normalized to GAPDH (A10868, Abclonal).

RNA sequencing for pancreatic cancer cells
For transcriptomic analysis, cells were treated with MB10 (0.64 μM), gemcitabine (0.50 μM), their combination, or DMSO as a vehicle control. Total RNA was extracted from PANC-1 cells using the Total RNA Extractor (Trizol) (B511311, Sangon Biotech) following the manufacturer's protocol. Libraries were prepared using the Illumina TruSeq RNA Sample Preparation Kit, following standard protocols. The constructed libraries were sequenced on Ran Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Raw sequencing data were processed using FastQC for quality control and trimmed with Fastp to remove low-quality reads and adaptors. The resulting clean reads were aligned to the human genome (GRCh38) using STAR aligner. Gene expression profiles were quantified with feature Counts. Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 (v1.34.0)8 with default parameters, and genes with absolute log fold change > 1 and adjusted p < 0.01 were defined as differentially expressed.

Phosphoproteomic profiling by LC–MS/MS
PANC cells were seeded 24 h before treatment and, at 60–70% confluency, treated with equal volumes of DMSO (control), 1 μM gemcitabine for 36 h. Cells were washed with ice-cold PBS, harvested by scraping and snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Frozen cell pellets were lysed in RIPA buffer (P0013B, Beyotime) supplemented with 1 mM PMSF (ST507, Beyotime) and 1× phosphatase inhibitor cocktail A (P1082, Beyotime). Lysates were sonicated on ice and centrifuged at 15,793 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Supernatants were collected as total protein extracts, and protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay (23225, Thermo Scientific). Equal amounts of protein were processed using the SP3 (single-pot solid-phase-enhanced sample preparation) method, including acetonitrile-induced binding to magnetic beads, ethanol and acetonitrile washes, reduction with dithiothreitol, alkylation with chloroacetamide, and digestion with Trypsin/LysC. Phosphopeptides were enriched using an IMAC phosphopeptide enrichment kit (A32992, Thermo Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Enriched peptides were desalted using SOLA™ SPE 96-well plates and dried in a vacuum concentrator prior to LC–MS/MS analysis. Peptides were separated on a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system coupled to an Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples were loaded onto a trap column and separated on a PepMap™ Neo analytical column (15 cm × 150 μm, 2 μm). Mobile phase A consisted of 0.1% formic acid in water and mobile phase B consisted of 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Current strategies for scRNA-seq analysis focus on differential expression analysis methods coupled with pathway enrichment analysis. However, genes with unchanged expression yet profoundly modified regulatory associations remain hard to detect. To address this knowledge gap, in this manuscript, Huang et al. introduces scDNS, a computational framework designed to quantify "network rewiring" in single-cell data. The authors combine Graph Attention Networks (GAT) with Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) to identify regulators whose functional impact stems from altered interaction patterns rather than changes in transcript abundance.
The concept is quite novel, which aims to identify key genes playing important roles during a certain altered condition without showing the commonly assumed expression changes. The study is well-structured, and provided benchmark against existing tools (VIPER, Milo, MELD, etc.). The tool also demonstrate broad utility across diverse research settings, including primary immunodeficiency (IRF4 mutation), viral infection (IFN and COVID-19), and oncology (Gemcitabine resistance in PDAC). The experimental validation of TIMM44 as a therapeutic target is also a highlight demonstrating the power and robustness of this computational tool. However, several major technical and computational points require clarification before publication.
Major Comments
1. Simulated perturbations
In methods “Simulation setup for benchmarking datasets”, the scDNS tool introduces perturbations in three ways (shuffle, multiply, mix). While this is ok, this form of perturbation results in dramatic statistical divergence that may not accurately reflect the structured, non-random rewiring of regulatory networks observed in actual pathological conditions. Can the authors add more ways of perturbation to mimic the diverse scenarios of gene changes in biological settings? In addition, only one single cell dataset is used, it would beneficial if the authors could include more scRNA-seq datasets.
2. Algorithmic overfit
In figure2e, scDNS achieve an AUC value of near 1.0 in simulated data while other softwares are around 0.5, which is quite poor. This result alerts that there is an overfitting problem here. The core point of scDNS is to quantify the differences in probability distributions using JSD divergence. The perturbation methods used, as also discussed above, directly maximizes the JSD value, creating an inherent "home-court advantage" for scDNS compared with other published methods.
3. Benchmark
Following the previous question, in figure 2e-g benchmarking, Milo and scDist showed near-zero sensitivity in identifying perturbed subpopulations in specific DGR (Differential Gene Relationship) scenarios, while scDNS perform very good. The baseline methods chosen for comparison (e.g., Milo, Augur, scDist, VIPER) were not originally engineered to detect statistical divergence caused by random shuffling.
Milo and scDist are optimized for detecting shifts in neighborhood abundance or inter-condition distances. VIPER relies on established regulon structures to infer protein activity. Evaluated against a perturbation scheme that mirrors the specific mathematical logic of scDNS, their performance decline is expected.
4. Potential bias of prior knowledge networks
The scDNS framework relies on integrating established databases (TRUST, STRING, KEGG, etc.) to construct the initial reference network. There is a concern regarding "research bias": the model might be predisposed to find perturbations in well-studied genes, while "orphan genes" with fewer known interactions remain undetectable.
How about the authors perform an experiment by randomly removing varying percentages (e.g., 20%-50%) of prior edges to assess the robustness of identifying key regulators (e.g., TP53)?
5. DGRs validation
The scDNS can detect both genes with altered expression levels (DGE) and, interestingly, genes with unchanged expression levels but altered regulatory networks (DGR). In figure4, JAK1 and WTAP is identified as DGRs, while in figure6, TIMM44 is also considered as a DGR. These gene show a little mRNA change but high network perturbation. Some experimental validation in a certain setting will significantly strengthen the analytical power of this tool.
6. In the lupus IFN-β and COVID-19 cohorts, analyses appear to be conducted primarily at the cell level with minimal explicit modelling of donor variation, clinical covariates, or batch structure, raising concerns about confounding and dominance by high-cell-count samples; donor- or sample-level summaries (pseudo-bulk/mixed-effects, leave-one-donor-out checks) are needed to demonstrate cohort-level robustness of key signals.
Minor Comments
1. The GAT model requires 10 iterations of training to ensure robustness. Please provide time and memory complexity benchmarks for datasets exceeding 10,000 cells to ensure the tool is scalable for current large cohort.
2. Indicate in the Methods how hyperparameters were selected (grid search, prior experience, or ad hoc choices).
3. The reported github link and code is not available.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This study introduces scDNS, a novel computational framework for identifying dysregulated gene regulatory interactions and prioritizing effector genes and cells in single-cell data. The authors demonstrate that scDNS can identify perturbed genes and cell populations across diverse biological contexts. However, several aspects of the methodology and interpretation require further clarification.
1. scDNS incorporates multiple interaction databases to construct the prior GIN, but the rationale for selecting these specific databases is unclear. Are these standard resources in the field, or were they chosen based on empirical testing? More importantly, the authors should demonstrate that incorporating the prior GIN actually improves performance through ablation analysis. Specifically, compare scDNS performance with and without the prior GIN (i.e., using only single-cell expression data) to justify the added complexity of integrating these databases.
2. When defining edges, scDNS uses the top 100 marker genes and housekeeping genes with high expression frequency. It is unclear whether 100 marker genes are sufficient or not. Sensitivity analysis is required here. Also, the negative edges are constructed using zero expression or random sampling, but I wonder if they could include some undetected interactions, and whether that would affect the performance of scDNS.
3. The authors train the GAT model 10 times with different random seeds and aggregate attention scores. However, it is unclear whether 10 runs are sufficient for stable estimation. The authors should report the variability of attention scores across runs (e.g., coefficient of variation or standard deviation) for both simulated and real data. This analysis would help users understand the robustness of the method and guide appropriate parameter settings.
4. scDNS computes both joint probability densities p(Gᵢ, Gⱼ) and conditional densities p(Gᵢ | Gⱼ), claiming each has distinct advantages. However, since conditional densities are derived from joint densities, they contain overlapping information. The authors should perform ablation studies comparing performance using (a) joint density only, (b) conditional density only, and (c) both combined. They should provide examples where each density type captures different biological signals, and clarify the claim that each performs differently in "high-density vs. low-density cell populations".
5. scDNS constructs cell-type-specific networks, making its results inherently dependent on cell type definitions. However, the robustness to cell type annotation choices is not evaluated. The paper uses Seurat standard clustering method, but the clustering could be very different based on different parameters or methods being used. The authors should demonstrate the findings from scDNS are reproducible across reasonable variations.
6. The authors should report the computational runtime and memory requirements of scDNS on datasets of varying sizes. As single-cell datasets increasingly exceed hundreds of thousands cells, users need to understand how runtime scales with the number of cells and genes, and whether the method is feasible for large-scale datasets.
7. The interpretation of gene rankings is inconsistent throughout the manuscript. For example,
• Line 206: IRF4 is called the "top perturbed regulator" but ranks 273
• Lines 266-268: JAK1 and WTAP are highlighted but have moderate ranks
The authors should clearly define what rank/p-value cutoff constitutes a "top" or "significant" signal. How should users interpret rankings (is rank 273 considered high)?
8. For the COVID-19 analysis, scDNS identifies disease-driven perturbation signals, but the consistency of these signals across patients is not clear. If scDNS is applied to individual patients separately, are the identified signals replicated across patients? What is the degree of inter-patient variability in perturbation signals? Is such variability technical, or driven by real biological variability? It would be nice if the authors can show that scDNS can identify patient-specific dysregulation patterns that relate to disease severity or outcome.
9. Both the COVID-19 and IFN-β PBMC analyses utilized datasets with batch effects, which may introduce technical variation. While the authors apply Harmony correction for UMAP visualization, scDNS operates on uncorrected count data. Is scDNA robust under such circumstances?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We sincerely thank all Reviewers for the careful evaluation of our manuscript and for the
constructive suggestions. We have substantially revised the manuscript to address the concerns
and to improve clarity, robustness, and reproducibility. For ease of navigation, responses to
Reviewer 2 start on page 15. Reviewer’s comments are marked in black while our replies are
indicatedinblue.
Overviewofthemajorrevisions:
In this revision, we (i) expanded the simulation engine with biologically structured perturbation
modes and repositioned simulations as stress tests (rather than head-to-head rankings), so that
they serve to validate scDNS under diverse rewiring scenarios; accordingly, we removed
cross-method comparisons in these simulations, since the compared tools were developed for

with previously reported COVID severity signatures? Also it is a bit ambiguous to
call them "high-response" genes cause a strong immune response is not equivalent to
Covid19 disease severity.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this constructive feedback. We agree that the term “high-
response” could be misinterpreted as implying a direct equivalence between the
magnitude of immune activation and COVID-19 severity. To avoid confusion, we have
revised the manuscript and now refer to these genes as “disease-driven perturbation
genes,” defined as genes showing the strongest scDNS-inferred network dysregulation
within each immune lineage.
(i) Gene lists.
To ensure full transparency, we now provide the complete lists of significant disease-
driven perturbation genes for each immune lineage (CD4⁺ T, CD8⁺ T, cycling NK/T-like,
and dendritic cells) in Supplementary Table 2.
(ii) Pathway enrichment.
We performed GO:BP and KEGG enrichment analyses and found that these lineage-
specific disease-driven genes are significantly enriched in immune processes highly
relevant to COVID-19 immunopathology (Response Fig. 1a; representative genes
annotated). Across lineages, the top enriched themes consistently point to immune
activation and effector programs, including cytokine- and interferon-related signaling,
regulation of T-cell activation, cytokine production (including TNF-related programs),
and regulation of inflammatory responses. Collectively, these enrichments indicate a
coordinated immune activation/dysregulation program characterized by heightened
inflammatory signaling and effector function.
To delineate shared core biology, we further derived a cross-lineage recurrent set
(genes present in ≥2 lineages) and repeated the enrichment analysis, which yielded
dominant terms related to leukocyte activation and positive regulation of
inflammatory response. These results support the conclusion that scDNS captures
severity-associated state transitions in immune cells.
(iii) Overlap with published COVID-19 severity signatures.
We note that a simple pooled, gene-by-gene overlap with previously reported
“severity signatures” can be misleading, because many published signatures are
derived from bulk/whole-blood analyses and can be strongly influenced by cell-
composition shifts (often including epithelial- or neutrophil-associated transcripts),
whereas our signatures are immune-lineage- and cell-state-resolved. Therefore, we do
not necessarily expect large one-to-one overlap across studies; instead, we emphasize
concordance at the level of biological processes/modules, where we observe
consistent enrichment for immune/leukocyte activation (Response Fig. 1b)—an
overarching theme widely linked to COVID-19 severity (PMID: 32788292, 32717743).
Nevertheless, as requested, we performed a direct overlap analysis using the union
gene set across the four immune lineages and observed partial intersections with an
established severe-versus-mild differential gene sets (31/1001, 3.1%) (PMID:
33096026)(Response Fig. 1c). Notably, the overlapping genes prominently included
interferon-response transcripts such as CD38, IFI44L, HERC5, and SIGLEC1 (CD169),
all
of which are well-established type I interferon–inducible genes and have been
consistently associated with heightened inflammation and severe COVID-19 (PMID:
33635833; 38772950; 41551039; 33825125; 36522333).
These revisions have been incorporated into the COVID-19 Results subsection (lines
331–334) and Supplementary Note 3 (lines 613–614).
Response Fig. 1 | Enrichment analysis and validation of high-scZscore cell
signatures. a, Functional enrichment of upregulated genes in high-scZscore cells
across major immune compartments. Bar plots show significantly enriched Gene
Ontology Biological Process terms and KEGG pathways for CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells,
Dendritic cells, and Cycling NK/T cells. The x-axis represents the enrichment
significance calculated as -log (adjusted P-values). Representative genes associated
10
with each term are listed below the bars. b, GOBP and KEGG enrichment analysis of
genes commonly upregulated in high-scZscore cells across at least two cell types. c,
Venn diagram illustrating the overlap between upregulated genes identified in high-
scZscore cells (scDNS-derived) and those associated with COVID-19 severity in a
benchmark multi-omic study (Overmyer et al., 2021, PMID: 33096026). The
intersection contains 31 common genes, representing a statistically significant overlap
(P = 0.002, hypergeometric test), highlighting the biological relevance of the scDNS-
identified cell populations to clinical disease severity.
(2). The authors stated that an independent bulk RNA-seq cohort was used for
validating the gene signature. But this cohort is not cited (either in rebuttal or Main
text). Please specify the source of this cohort.
Response：
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. The independent bulk
RNA-seq cohort used to validate the high-response gene signature is GSE217948
(Wang, Y. et al., Front. Immunol. 13:1043219, 2023). Although this dataset was already
cited in the main text, we agree it was not sufficiently prominent. We have now added
the citation at the first mention of the bulk validation in the revised manuscript and
also included it in the relevant Data Availability section.
(3). The interpretation of outlier C53ctr as having an 'unrecognized infection-related
immune state' is plausible but speculative. Is clinical metadata available to support
this?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important point. We agree that our previous
interpretation of C53ctr as having an “unrecognized infection-related immune state”
was overly specific given the absence of direct infection evidence. Upon re-
examination of the clinical annotations, donor C53ctr shows multiple comorbidities
and respiratory manifestations, including pre-existing lung disease (e.g., asthma/COPD,
requiring home O₂, any chronic lung condition), pre-existing diabetes, prior smoking,
and respiratory symptoms (see Supplementary Table S1 of the original study,
https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-021-03569-
1/MediaObjects/41586_2021_3569_MOESM4_ESM.xlsx).
We have therefore revised the manuscript to describe C53ctr more conservatively as
an immune-activated/inflammatory outlier. This is consistent with the elevated
expression of genes involved in antigen processing, MHC assembly, and related
immune programs in C53ctr compared with the other healthy controls
(Supplementary Note Fig. 2g-j). Our donor-aware analyses confirm that this signal is
not explained by technical covariates (e.g., UMI counts, detected genes), supporting a
biological basis. As we demonstrated in last revision, this outlier illustrates donor-level
heterogeneity captured by scDNS but does not alter our main cohort-level conclusions.
